lesson.title: A World War Begins on the Frontier: The French and Indian War
lesson.summary: Fighting between Britain and France over the Ohio Valley escalated into the French and Indian War of 1754 to 1763, a conflict that redrew the map of North America and left Britain deep in debt, with major consequences for its colonies.
lesson.body:
French exploration of North America over the previous century and a half, from Jacques Cartier's voyages up the St. Lawrence River in the 1530s to Samuel de Champlain's founding of Quebec in 1608 and La Salle's expeditions down the Mississippi later in the 1600s, had given France a claim to a vast interior territory stretching from Canada down through the Ohio Valley to Louisiana. By the early 1750s, French forces began building a chain of forts in the Ohio River Valley to secure this claim and to link Canada with Louisiana, directly threatening British colonial claims to the same territory, including land claimed by Virginia and its land speculators.

Fighting broke out in 1754 when a young Virginia militia officer named George Washington, sent to warn the French away from the region, led a small force that ambushed a French scouting party at a place called Jumonville Glen. The French later forced Washington to surrender at nearby Fort Necessity that summer, an early defeat that nonetheless marked the opening clash of what colonists came to call the French and Indian War, so named from the British colonial perspective because Britain fought against both French forces and many of France's Native American allies. That same year, delegates meeting at Albany had proposed the Albany Plan of Union partly to coordinate colonial defense against exactly this kind of French threat, but the plan's rejection meant the colonies entered the war still largely uncoordinated.

The war expanded into a series of major campaigns across the following years. In 1755, British general Edward Braddock led a large force to capture Fort Duquesne in the Ohio Valley but was killed and his army routed in a disastrous ambush. The tide turned in Britain's favor later in the war, particularly after William Pitt took charge of British war strategy and committed greater resources to North America. British and colonial forces captured the French fortress of Louisbourg in 1758, and in September 1759 British general James Wolfe defeated French general the Marquis de Montcalm outside Quebec City in a battle in which both commanders were mortally wounded, a turning point that led to the fall of Montreal in 1760 and effectively ended French resistance in Canada.

Beyond North America, this same conflict formed the American theater of a much larger global struggle between Britain, France, and their respective allies, generally known as the Seven Years' War, fought across Europe, the Caribbean, India, and West Africa between 1756 and 1763. The war finally ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1763, in which France ceded Canada and all its territory east of the Mississippi River to Britain, while transferring Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain, effectively removing France as a major colonial power on the North American mainland.

Victory came at a steep price. Britain had spent enormous sums fighting the war and now had to pay for defending and administering a vastly larger North American empire, including a frontier where the war had inflamed rather than resolved tensions with Native nations. Looking for ways to cover this debt and to manage the newly won territory, British ministers turned their attention toward the colonies themselves, setting the stage for a new era of frontier policy and taxation, beginning with the Proclamation of 1763, that would ultimately push Britain and its American colonies toward the crisis of revolution.
